title: Selection Sorts Differences That Already Exist

scenes.tts: In nineteen seventy-seven, a severe drought struck Daphne Major, a small island in the Galápagos. Most of its medium ground finches died. The birds left had deeper beaks, on average. Researchers had measured them before the drought. So did the drought change the birds, or change which were left?

scenes.tts: Natural selection needs three things at once. First, variation. Variation means the differences among individuals. Second, inheritance. An inherited trait is carried in genes from parent to young. Third, unequal success. The differences change how many offspring an individual leaves. A mutation is a change in DNA. It is the source of new versions of genes. Selection does not make variation. It sorts the variation that is there, including new mutations as they arise.
scenes.visual: Three rows: varied beaks, parent to young with same beak, one bird with more young; a DNA bar with one block changing; a sorter.

scenes.tts: Fitness is how many offspring an individual leaves that survive to reproduce. An adaptation is an inherited trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its present environment. On Daphne Major, a deep beak was an adaptation. Large birds, especially males with large beaks, survived best. They could crack the large, hard seeds left after the drought.

scenes.tts: No bird's beak grew because of the drought. The birds that died were, on average, different from the birds that lived. Beak size is strongly inherited, so the next generation's beaks were deeper too, on average. Over many generations, selection like this can make a population better suited to its environment, but not perfectly suited. In later years, selection on these finches changed direction as rainfall and seeds changed.

scenes.tts: How can one species become two? A species is a group of populations whose members interbreed and produce fertile offspring in nature, and that rarely breed with other groups. Speciation is when one species splits into groups that no longer do that, or only rarely do. It often starts with geographic isolation. That is a barrier, such as a river, between the groups. On each side, different mutations arise and different traits are favoured. Separation alone is not speciation, though.
scenes.visual: One species box; a river splits it; each side changes in a different way; the river fades with a question.
scenes.narration: How can one species become two? A species is a group of populations whose members interbreed and produce fertile offspring in nature, and that rarely breed with other groups. Speciation is when one species splits into groups that no longer do that, or only rarely do. It often starts with geographic isolation. That is a barrier, such as a river, between the groups. On each side, different mutations arise and different traits are favoured. Separation alone is not speciation, though.

scenes.tts: Back to the question. The drought did not reshape any finch's beak. It changed which birds lived to breed. Their young inherited deeper beaks. One species can become two when separated groups change in different ways until they no longer interbreed. Selection sorts the differences that already exist.
